utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That affirmation you made at the beginning of your evidence still applies, of course.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic. Ah; Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Wheeler. My name is Momcilo Bulatovic. I am one of Mr. Sljivancanin's Defence counsel, as you probably know, and I will be asking you a number of questions on behalf of Mr. Sljivancanin's team, questions which I believe to be relevant both in terms of our defence strategy and also in order to understand the totality of your report. First of all, Mr. Wheeler, something you talked about yesterday. What I want to know about is the source of your information, the source of your knowledge that went into the production of your report. You referred to newspaper articles, but I want to know if there was anything else that you used; secondary or primary literature, which authors, and over which period of time exactly.

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me start with the final part of your question. I wrote the report in the -- in December, 1997, and at the beginning of January, 1998. It was done rather quickly. There hadn't been that much time before I was asked to serve as an expert witness and needing to produce the report. It was based almost entirely on secondary sources, that is accounts by journalists and the published literature that already existed in book form. Aside from materials which were provided to me by the Prosecution, many of which related to publications in Croatia that had already appeared, memoir literature relating to the siege in Vukovar, I can't remember very many of the names of the authors, I must admit, at this stage, and I was not asked to provide footnotes in the report. Apparently that's not the common practice in courts of law, although of course it would be for any academic paper. And the lapse of time means that it's very difficult for me now to remember where specific facts or allegations that I record in the paper, where exactly they came from. I have to admit that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, the newspaper articles you used, when were these published; the period relevant for our indictment or later on, given the fact that you drafted and produced your report in 1997 and not earlier?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of the newspaper reports were, of course, contemporary to the events. There was quite a bit of newspaper coverage, of course, of the siege and fall of Vukovar. Others, of course, were retrospective accounts of the events of how the war came to Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, I heard you say yesterday - and that is part of your report, too - that the public media on both sides, the Croat side and the Serb side, provided, for the most part, biased commentary. Did you perhaps at any point in time have any second thoughts about the information you used and about your sources?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER [Resumed]
utterances.text: One always has second thoughts about using journalistic sources as an historian, but if you're trying to write what amounts to contemporary history, journalistic sources, newspaper sources are among the best. As regarding whether or not Serbian and Croatian media in particular were biased or prejudiced, it should be said that the nationalistic fervor and the spreading of fear and hate that I did refer to a couple of times yesterday was not characteristic of the entire media scene either in Zagreb or Belgrade. There were, of course, noble exceptions then, newspapers and radio stations that sought to be fair and honest, but one, of course -- if one were, as I was, living and working abroad, my most regular source of information would have been the foreign press, particularly the press in the United Kingdom. I used to, of course also -- I mean, I used to read things from the former Yugoslavia. I read Vreme regularly, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Aside from Vreme, did you consult any other magazines from Serbia, or did you only consult the press from Serbia as far as the Yugoslav Federation at the time was concerned, and was this only based on what you could read in the Vreme magazine?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned Vreme because it was the one magazine I subscribed to myself, but of course I would use the -- the BBC's monitoring service to read translations of a wide variety of articles from other Yugoslav publications across the federation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Wheeler, before you eventually produced this report pursuant to a request from the OTP, and in a hasty fashion, as you have pointed out yourself, did you ever talk directly, did you interview any of those involved in what was going on back in 1990 and 1991? And I mean anyone from the top level leadership down to the grassroots, as it were, be it in Serbia or in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Although, because I had lived in Vukovar itself in the spring of 1997, I did meet quite a few of the leaders of the -- the new Samostalna Srpska Demokratska Stranka. But our concern at that point had nothing to do with the origins of the war and everything to do with the forthcoming elections in Croatia in April 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever interview any Croatian citizens or did you perhaps use any sources produced by Croatian statesmen or politicians, such as memoirs, interviews, collections of interviews, that sort of thing?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not for this report. Most of the most interesting ones of those appeared later, if we're talking about people like Sarinic and so forth. Those were not available to me at the time. In any case, of course, the thrust of the report had been to sketch in the historical background, not to provide a blow-by-blow, if you will, account of the war in Eastern Slavonia. The bulk of the paper, of course, relates to historical background. Historical background, I said, not local background.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You will agree, Mr. Wheeler, that this historical background in the former Yugoslavia was indeed quite a complex one, not to put too fine a point on it, won't you?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly would.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Wheeler, I read your report, and I came across a number of things that I find particularly interesting and which I would like to ask you to clarify. You speak about King Aleksandar in 1921, when the dictatorship was introduced in a bid to save his empire, and then you say there was a negligible number of Croats to become more important later on who then founded an Ustasha terrorist organisation. Can you explain about this negligible number of Croats and where they came from. We can start with that and then proceed with everything else, please.

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, the King introduced his dictatorship in 1929, which -- not 1921. This led to the formation by Ante Pavelic of his Ustasha movement. He had been a former Member of Parliament. At this beginning, his followers were very, very few, probably no more than a few hundred, and his followers very quickly were harried out of Yugoslavia, and he took up residence as an effective guest of Mussolini in Italy. Later on, his people were trained for the assassination plot on King Aleksandar, that plot that culminated in the successful murder of Aleksandar in Marseilles in October, 1934. Many of these hitmen were not just Croats, of course, they were also Bulgarian VMRO people, Macedonian revolutionary terrorist organisation, and they had been largely trained and supplied with armaments in Hungary. So the plot against Aleksandar exemplified both the enmity or hatred felt towards the Yugoslav Kingdom both by some of its neighbours but also by this minority of radical Croats suffused with fascist sympathies who represented a radical departure from the Starcevic sort of nationalism of the 19th century. They claimed themselves to be followers of the Party of Right of Starcevic, but of course they were extremely radical versions of anything that one might have called Pravastvo, or rightism, in the Croatian political firmament.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I did say 1921 -- or, rather, 1929. So that's an error in the transcript. Line 5, page 9, [as interpreted] I think. Sir, I now want to know about this radical organisation, the Ustasha terrorist radical organisation. At which point in time did it acquire any degree of significance in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It never had any political significance until Hitler decided to put it in power in April, 1941. Like terrorist organisations anywhere, it was capable of the odd outrage, putting bombs on -- in -- in the lavatories on railway trains, for example. It liked to do that sort of thing. But it took only a very few people to accomplish what, in retrospect, seem like rather naive outrages but were significant for the time. Its political significance depended upon the patronage that it ultimately won from Mussolini and Hitler, most of all Hitler.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: This is something you mentioned yesterday. If you'd please elaborate. Why did Hitler want to have an Ustasha terrorist organisation like that in power? Why did he want to reward them so richly in a way? Is this about the antagonism between the Germans on the one hand and the Serbs on the other because of what had occurred during World War II? And the perspective that I'm putting this into is the enemies surrounding Serbia itself.

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you of course meant to say World War I, not World War II. Yes. The important point to make is that actually Hitler didn't want to put Pavelic and the Ustasha in power. He would have much preferred to have done a deal with Vlatko Macek and the Croatian Peasant Party. He wanted a secure Croatia, but Macek and the overwhelming majority of the Croatian Peasant Party refused to receive an independent Croatia or a nominally independent Croatia as a gift from Hitler. Strenuous efforts had been made by Axis diplomats to seduce Macek and the Croatian Peasant Party. Although he did leave politics in protest at the Mirkovic-Simovic coup, the Croatian Peasant Party nonetheless remained in government. And it was because the Croatian Peasant Party would not accept the role of being the stooge rulers of Croatia for the axis powers that Hitler had to fall back upon what he had originally seen as Mussolini's protege, that is Pavelic. Pavlovic was the only one, it seemed, to be available to run an axis satellite state of Croatia, and of course it was a decision which, from the axis's own point of view, was a disaster, because instead of ensuring peace, order, and the exploitation of the economic assets and the transport infrastructure, which is what Hitler wanted, instead the advent of Pavelic created exactly what the Germans didn't want, which was huge resistance and chaos and disruption of economic activity. And the transcript says "Pavlovic." It's Pavelic. Pavelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Wheeler, between 1934 and 1941, Yugoslavia was ruled by Prince Paul. You say that he made a peace pact, a separate peace pact with the largest Croatian party. What is the largest Croatian party that you have referred to and what sort of a separate peace pact would that be?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the largest and most significant Croatian party at the was indeed Macek's Croatian Peasant Party, which at that point, of course, had been before the advent of Prince Paul and the doing of the Sporazum deal. Macek had been allied with Pribicevic and the Independent Democratic Party, the party of Serbs of Croatia in the anti-dictatorship pact. But I referred to the Sporazum, the Cvetkovic-Macek Agreement, as a separate piece because it detached Macek's Croatian Peasant Party from the unified pro-democracy bloc that actually united Serbs, Croats, and Slovenes in the latter stages of King Aleksandar's dictatorship. Macek agreeing with Prince Paul on a devolved home rule system for Croatia had the effect of weakening tremendously the democratic opposition to the dictatorship across the entire country.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, in relation to World War II, Germany's invasion and the carving up of the occupied countries, you say this is something that Hitler came up with with the intention of forever destroying even the very idea of Yugoslavia and in order to introduce an effective system of occupation during World War II. From a purely historical viewpoint, can you explain Hitler's plan to me, please, especially his intention to forever destroy even the very idea of a Yugoslav state. How could he possibly have this implemented? With whose assistance and how far did they eventually get?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, his intention was given effect by the way in which he partitioned the country, giving slices of territory to the Hungarians, the Bulgarians, the phoney, fake Albanian state, which was effectively ruled by the Italians, giving the Italians the Dalmatian coast, creating Montenegro as a supposedly independent kingdom under the house of Savoy, that is the Italian monarchy. The system failed because none of these recipients of Hitler's generosity or largesse, including the Croats with their supposedly independent Croatian state, were happy with the results. Either they wanted much more territory than they got, or, for example, in the case of the Bulgarians being given the right to occupy -- occupy Macedonia, Vardar, Macedonia, they didn't actually get title to it. So they were dissatisfied even though there wasn't necessarily, until late in the war, very much trouble for them in that part of the world. So instead of replacing an orderly occupation regime -- excuse me instead of creating an orderly occupation regime, Hitler found himself presiding over what amounted to a hideously disorderly occupation regime which ended up demanding the presence of vastly more axis troops and also ultimately demanding far more intimate relations with various collaboration forces than Hitler had intended. His animosity towards the idea of a Yugoslav state, towards the idea particularly of a Serb-dominated Yugoslav state does indeed go back, as you rather suggested, to longstanding Germanic animosity towards the Serbs as a dangerous and strong people. And, you know, Hitler had racial notions, a racial ranking of people who were acceptable and not acceptable. In the South Slav context, this meant that he regarded the Slovenes, for example, as genetically sufficiently decent people to be suitable for Germanisation. But for Serbs, as for, for example, Poles or Ukrainians, the only real solution was to make slaves out of them. For Croats, on the other hand, it was rather an embarrassing situation. Obviously the Croats are Slavs but the Ustasha regime had to seek to invent for itself a supposedly Aryan, non-Slav genealogy, racial descent, that is, which of course was ludicrous beyond belief, but in order to fit into Hitler's world view, mad as it was, it was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me, what sort of an influence did the Catholic church have on all of this?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not, it has to be said, a very positive impact upon all of this. This remains, of course, an extremely controversial question historically. The Catholic church traditionally in Croatia and, for that matter, in Slovenia and in Bosnia-Herzegovina, was leaving aside some of the Franciscans in the northern parts of Bosnia. This Catholic church was traditionally extremely conservative and extremely nationalistic, and a good many Croatian Catholic priests and even a couple of bishops, notoriously the Bishop of Mostar, for example, went over to the Ustasha. Some priests even resigned as priests and became Ustasha gauleiters - I forget the term - and then were leaders of Ustasha bands. The hierarchy of the church, of course, led by Archbishop Alojz Stepinac equivocated. It on the one hand protested regularly, but, unfortunately, privately, to Pavelic and the Ustasha regime about the persecution of non-Croats. But on the other hand it was also rather gratified by the opportunity to increase the size of its flock by virtue of the conversions that took place. Stepinac, was, we understand, unhappy and nervous about forced conversions, but he nonetheless rather liked the idea of creating more Catholics. And history has not treated him very well outside of Croatia, of course, where he has been inappropriately, in my view, promoted to a would-be saint, but history abroad has not been very kind of him, not because he was a bad man but because he was a weak man and failed to rise to the spiritual and moral standard that one might have expected of the leading Roman Catholic prelate in Croatia, or among the Croats. As I said, there were other priests and junior bishops who were very, very much more morally compromised by their wartime behaviour than was Stepinac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the conversion of Serbs, Mr. Wheeler. Perhaps do you know the number of Serbs who were converted in this way?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know the number, and I don't know that we do have an exact number. And at the moment, I can't even recall what some of the more significant estimates might have been, but we're certainly talking of something around -- well, at least a hundred thousand, maybe more. Some -- some of these conversions were in fact arranged between Catholic and Orthodox priests simply in order to provide protection for people. Other conversions were actually -- and everybody realised they were fake conversions. They were just designed to save people's lives. But in other places, of course, the conversions were not done in that benign and in fact rather helpful way. But the exact number I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Wheeler. Again, in your statement or report there is an assertion that the Serbs from the very beginning were separated for deserved punishment. Could you please explain to us, what does that mean "from the beginning," and what would be the "deserved punishment," and why would they be singled out in particular and what would be the reason for that?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly didn't write that the punishment was deserved. I wrote condign punishment. That means, in English, special punishment, especially harsh punishment. And the Serbs were singled out for that punishment because they were regarded by the Axis powers as the most dangerous people in Yugoslavia, the ones who had committed the insult of the 27th of March coup d'etat, the slap in the face of Hitler, the people who were seen as traditional enemies of the German race, and therefore the people who had to be treated most harshly, not just because the Serbs were thought to be dangerous but also as a lesson to all the other Yugoslav peoples of what the price would be -- what the price was that would have to be paid if you didn't behave, because the word "condign" also implies a useful lesson. The Serbs would be punished in order to keep Slovens, Bosnian Muslims, Croats, Slavs in Macedonia, Serbs would be punished to keep them in line and to remind the others of how well they were having it or how -- I put that badly. To remind the others of how much worse it could be if they followed in the supposedly bad Serbian example of opposing the interests of the Reich. You know, it has to be said as well that Hitler's aim was simply to stoke up as much hatred as possible amongst the South Slav peoples. If you reward some and punish others, the effect, of course, is to make those other -- make those people dislike each other even more. This was part of his aim, as I said, to destroy the idea of a future Yugoslav state.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Can I take it, then, Mr. Wheeler, from what you've just said that that's where the roots are of the implementation of a genocidal policy in the spring of 1941, which then prompted the Serbs to a rebellion which began in Eastern Herzegovina? Could you please explain this policy. Who implemented it at the expense of whom?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The policy is -- was implemented from May, 1941, onwards by the new Ustasha regime. It was their idea, their plan. It was carried out by their bands of cut-throats and by the Ustasha themselves, not by what became the Croatian army, the so-called Domobranci. This provoked, as you suggested, fervent and natural Serb opposition where it was implemented, caused the outbreak of resistance, and as I said yesterday, also eventually produced so much chaos that Hitler himself, far from thinking it was a good idea, tried to get it stopped, although again the -- it's very difficult talking sensibly in some cases about the Axis powers in the Second World War because the policies implemented on the ground by particular German or Italian generals could vary significantly from orders delivered, for example, from either Rome or Berlin. So the specifics -- I'm generalising, but I want to issue a health warning, if you will, that sometimes the specifics in given areas, because of individual personalities and the policies they adopted, could vary. So in other words, in some places there might be German units that supported the Ustasha genocide, in other areas there would be German units that opposed it. In most cases the Italians, fortunately for their historical reputation, opposed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't hear, Mr. Wheeler, who were the victims of genocide of these Ustasha cut-throat groups, or bands, as you described them.

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course in -- in numerical terms, the Serbs were the largest victims, but the Ustasha was as profoundly anti-Semitic as was Hitler himself and so the Jews of Yugoslavia, particularly the Jews of the Independent State of Croatia, were also targets for liquidation, as, of course, were other "untermenschen" such as Gypsies; Roma. There would have been other targets for the genocide had patriarchal values in south-eastern Europe been such in 1941 that Pavelic, for example, could have conceived of the idea of homosexuality. If he had, they would have also been victims, such people. But Serbs, Jews and Gypsies were the principal opponents -- excuse me, were the principal victims, as of course eventually were anti-fascist Croats, particularly those associated with or in the Communist Party or who joined the Partisan resistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Would we agree, then, Mr. Wheeler, on the basis of what you have said so far today, that Yugoslavia was something that the Serbs needed, that it was their idea, it was their desire to live in a state that they called Yugoslavia for the reasons you cited, and that in that state Croatia, Slovenia had separatist tendencies because this life together with Serbs, Gypsies, Jews was something that did not suit them?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As I explained yesterday, the original inventors of the Yugoslav idea were Croats. There were also eventually, by the end of the 19th century, many ardent Slovenes in favour of the idea of a Yugoslav state, as there were by the end of the 19th century also many Serbian intellectuals in favour of the Yugoslav state. When I said that the Yugoslav state best served the interests of the Serbs, what I meant to convey was the fact that the sort of Yugoslavia that came into existence in 1918 and then under its constitution of 1921 tended to pay better attention to or to serve better Serb interests than it was seen by Slovenes or Croats as serving their interests. They didn't feel they had the common state they had wanted. They felt that they had an expanded Serbian state where they -- it would be too strong to say that they felt like they were second-class citizens, but they did feel they had legitimate grievances because the Yugoslavia, the sort of Yugoslavia that they had wanted had not come into existence. And they felt that the Serbs as the people of state who were most numerous, had the longest recent experience of independent political life, were dominating them. This feeling, of course, was vastly more pronounced amongst the Croats during the inter-war period than it was amongst the Slovenes. The remarkable thing about what was going to happen during the 1980 and 1990s was that the Slovenes for the first time would start to believe that they needed a separate existence. They had entertained no such ideas previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: And does that mean, Mr. Wheeler, precisely what I said before, that the idea of breaking up Yugoslavia is not a Serbian idea but a Croatian or a Slovenian idea, idea of those who did not achieve or think they did not manage to achieve the importance and the place they would expect to have by joining a community of the type that Yugoslavia was?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we run the risk here of joining together the very different inter-war experiences with the experience after Tito's death and the progressive decline of legitimacy and belief in the socialist Yugoslav state. For -- in the case of the socialist Yugoslav state and its decline and dissolution and ultimate resort to warfare, the lead was certainly taken by the Milosevic regime in Belgrade. It was the Milosevic regime in Belgrade which was seen by the other Yugoslav peoples to be trying to change the rules of the federation in a way which would be disadvantageous to them. The Slovenes were the first people to realise the way in which Yugoslavia, the sort of Yugoslavia that Milosevic appeared to want, that this Yugoslavia was not a state in which they wanted to live. The Slovenes, therefore, were the first of the people to -- first of the Yugoslav peoples to decide that they might have to leave. But as I tried to emphasise yesterday, the crisis of 1989, 1990, 1991, which gets more and more tense, didn't then look as if it would inevitably lead to the break-up of Yugoslavia. I tried to make the -- for example, there are -- there are lots of public opinion poll evidence showing that in Slovenia, for example, even in the first half of 1991, although the government had actually scheduled an independence declaration on the 25th of June, most people didn't actually think it was going to happen. They thought they were engaged in yet another and more -- and more energetic process of negotiation or of bluffing. So more and more non-Serbs do indeed, in the later 1980s and beginning of the 1990s, consider leaving Yugoslavia, but for most of them their preference is in fact a different sort of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Isn't it indicative, Mr. Wheeler -- well, earlier you said that the Slovenians in that first state, in the kingdom, were the first who wanted to leave the kingdom because they did not manage to achieve some of their interests and it didn't suit them. Now, in the case of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, Slovenians again were dissatisfied. Does that mean that their participation in a community called Yugoslavia, they were unsatisfied -- dissatisfied with their position there and they kept wanting to leave that community? Yugoslavia was something that did not suit them; they did not manage to fulfil this ambitions, to achieve some of their objectives, some of their desires. What would you say?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, your characterisation of the Slovene position in the late 1980s and early 1990s I would agree with, but not your characterisation of Slovene descent in the inter-war years, during the kingdom. The Slovenes by and large did very well out of their position in the Kingdom of Yugoslavia. In the first place, of course, it saved them from either Italian or Austrian or German Imperialism. It saved their territory from being gobbled up by either Italy or Germany or Austria. So Slovenes were relatively content, really, in the inter-war years. They got on with making money, being prosperous, being efficient, being happy. Their language protected them. Their separate language protected them from many of the measures which annoyed Croats who, of course, shared a language with the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Wheeler, I'm now going to go back to a topic -- actually, I'm going to move to a topic which touches upon what we talked about already, and that concerns the order of the then state, the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and one of its segments. I don't know how much you studied that. We're talking about the armed forces of the SFRY. Do you know what the armed forces of the SFRY consisted of according to the 1974 constitution?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally, yes, but I do not pretend to be anyone who knows a great deal about the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that as part of the armed forces of the SFRY, according to the 1974 constitution, which you say that you've read - and if you recall it, then that's very well - that the Yugoslav People's Army and the Territorial Defence make up the armed forces of the SFRY? Is that something that you are aware of?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. I'm aware of all the ideas of All People's National Defence and so forth as they became -- as they were propagated in the latter years of Tito's lifetime.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: During Josip Broz Tito's lifetime, he was the Supreme Commander of the armed forces of that state which was called what it was called; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: After he died, do you know who assumed the command and control of the armed forces of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed; the command was shared by the collective Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us, if you know, and you probably know because this was something that you studied, who made up this collective Presidency? How many members did it have, and who was the president during the time relevant for the indictment? Who was the president of that Presidency and how many members did it have?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It had one member from each of the six republics plus a member from each of Serbia's two autonomous provinces, plus a member who was the -- the Secretary-General of the Communist Party, League of Communists, and there was a military member.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: During the -- the time relevant for the period of the indictment, do you know who was the chief of the Presidency or the president of the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The president of the Presidency in the early part of 1991 was Borisav Jovic. He resigned, and then went back. Then after a crisis over whether or not Stipe Mesic should succeed, who was next in line, the candidate from Croatia, Mesic eventually did assume the -- the role of president of the Presidency following European Community intervention in end of June, beginning of July, 1991. So during the period of the siege of Vukovar, the notional president of the Presidency was Stipe Mesic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You're absolutely right, Mr. Wheeler. He was the president of the Presidency from the 30th of June until the 3rd of October, 1991. In the media, and you probably followed the media, a news item was published that Mr. Mesic, after he left the Presidency in the way that he left it - I'm not going to go into that, but if necessary, I will explain it - he said, "I have completed my work. Yugoslavia is no more, and I am going back." Do you remember this, Mr. Wheeler?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do indeed. He even titled his first volume of memoirs, "Kako Smo Srusili Jugoslaviju."

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I see that you did look at the book by Mr. Mesic, and you are familiar with it. Did you use that book in order to draft your expert findings?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't have a copy of it then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes. Sorry, Your Honour, but for the record, could we have the name of the book in English? It was given in B/C/S but it wasn't translated into English.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's "How --" "How We Destroyed Yugoslavia," although the second edition doesn't say "we," I believe. It says "How Yugoslavia Was Destroyed," or "How Yugoslavia Was Destroyed." I can't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the name of the book is really not that important to me, but what is important to me is that you are familiar with the statement by Mr. Mesic and that this is something that is beyond dispute. What I'm interested in is the attitude of Croatia towards that community by the name of Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia of which he was the president of the Presidency. Mr. Wheeler, do you know what the 1974 constitution, even though perhaps you're not the right person to ask that, but in this entire historical context and following all the events through the constitutional framework and the constitutional solutions, what were the tasks of the armed forces of the SFRY as provided for by the constitution, or if you would like me to remind you what it states in Article 240 of the constitution, perhaps we can deal with that. What it states there is that the armed forces of the SFRY protect the sovereignty, independence, territorial integrity of Yugoslavia and the social order established by this constitution. Do you recall that part of the constitution from 1974 as it relates to the armed forces of the SFRY?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly do, and you will find in my report that I refer explicitly to the obligation of the JNA not only to defend the country but also to defend its social system. That is self-management socialism.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: What I'm interested in is another obligation of the armed forces, and that is the territorial integrity aspect. Could you please clarify that duty that the armed forces have. What could you say about that as it relates to territorial integrity?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Any country's armed forces would be charged with defending that state's territorial integrity. In the Yugoslav context, of course, it becomes vastly more problematic when the state is in the process of dissolution and one or another of its component parts is seeking secession. That indeed does put the -- an army, charged with defending the territorial integrity of the country, in a difficult position.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, the country was well on its way to disintegration. That much is certain, and there's no need to discuss it. What I want to know is did the armed forces take part in making political decisions or were the armed forces only there to carry out the orders of whoever was in command? During his lifetime, Tito was the Supreme Commander and now it was the Presidency. So did the army have any bearing on political decisions or was it only there to implement whatever decisions were taken at the political level by the political leaders of the country?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The army had, and certainly in these years of crisis, took an increasingly explicit political role. General Kadijevic, the minister of defence, and his successors did take an active part in the politics of the time. And the disarray that prevailed in the collective Presidency meant in fact there was greater scope for the army to play an explicitly political role.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Wheeler, you think the army took an active role in this. The question is why? Was it in order to preserve the Yugoslav community, the SFRY, or to get involved in its break-up? I'm not talking about what happened later. I'm talking about the political decisions and the army's involvement in that. Do you know specifically what the involvement was of Mr. Kadijevic and his successors in terms of Yugoslavia being preserved, Yugoslavia being brought down, and Yugoslavia eventually disappearing from the map?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Kadijevic was among those who believed that it was essential to proclaim martial law in order to stop the slide towards dissolution. He tried to get that in early March, I think it was, 1991, through the collective Presidency, was refused, rebuffed in very dramatic scenes which of course we've all actually seen the pictures of, you know, with the pressure being exerted on Bogic Bogicevic, for example, the representative from Bosnia. All very dramatic stuff. But it illustrates the extent to which the army was desperately seeking to save the state which it was pledged to defend, a state which was, despite the army's ethos, purpose of existence, loyalty, a state which was falling apart around the army that existed to defend and protect that state. It was for the top brass, as well as many ordinary officers, I imagine, an incredibly, incredibly difficult period. They're watching a country disintegrate that the army exists to protect.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, I entirely agree with you. Do you know whose insignia the JNA men were wearing at the time? Were those Yugoslav insignia or republican insignia?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER [Resumed]
utterances.text: They wore Yugoslav insignia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Wheeler, here we have Mr. Kadijevic. You've mentioned him. Do you know what this person's ethnicity was?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a Serb from Croatia. I believe he was also the product of a mixed marriage. I can't remember which way around it was, though. He considered himself a Serb from Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: A Serb from Croatia, you say. The question of his ethnicity. Do you know what the ethnic make-up was of the officers in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is a difficult question to answer because, off the top of my head, I don't have the figures, but it is a difficult question to answer for other reasons as well because it depends on what part of the officer corps you're talking about. Now, obviously conscripts represented the young men of Yugoslavia in the exact proportion that they actually existed in the country, so it was completely an integrated army. The lower level officer corps tended to be dominated by Serbs and Montenegrins for whom, traditionally, a career in the army was more attractive than it was for other South Slav peoples. At the highest levels, however, the army was also representative of the Yugoslav populations at large. So the proportion of Croatian generals and so forth would have been roughly equivalent to that of Serbs, Montenegrins, Bosnian Muslims, Slovenes, and so forth. The one conspicuous exception at the upper level would have been Albanians. Albanians, there would have been very few senior Albanian officers. But there were some. Part of the reason for the predominance of Serbs and Montenegrins at middle levels in the army was not just, of course, as I referred to before, the tradition of going into the army amongst those peoples being stronger, especially for those young men who came from relatively poor areas, it was also the fact that the army was a vast bureaucracy, much of which was located in Belgrade, and so therefore naturally "cinovnici," officials, would nonetheless wear a uniform, would have been disproportionately Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Wheeler, yesterday you said something that caught my eye, as it were. You said that back in 1991, it wasn't popular to be pro-Yugoslavia, to be of pro-Yugoslav orientation. Can you please try to elaborate on that. You did explain that to some degree yesterday, but I believe that further elucidations might be required. Who was this in the way of? Which were the bodies that so opposed this pro-Yugoslav orientation?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's necessary -- it's necessary to bear in mind that a pro-Yugoslav orientation suffered from the general decline which the Yugoslav state economy and political order had suffered after Tito's death. The Yugoslav state was no longer delivering to the bulk -- or excuse me, I shouldn't say the bulk. It was no longer delivering to many of its citizens what a state is obliged to deliver, which is a sense of prosperity, security, a functioning economy, a political order, a political system that people can believe in. In other words, the socialist regime was losing its legitimacy, and since the socialist regime was losing its legitimacy, to a considerable extent the common state represented by that socialist regime was losing legitimacy. When I remarked about it was unpopular to be pro-Yugoslav in 1991, I may have had in mind, however, the way in which the number of people who declared themselves as Yugoslavs - Yugoslavs by national identity - in the 1991 census had fallen on what the number had been in 1981, for example, in the immediate aftermath of Tito's death when people were feeling extremely patriotic and very pro-Yugoslav, or had been the case in 1971 when, because of the Russian invasion of Czechoslovakia, Yugoslav patriotism and optimism and excitement were also very, very great. So by 1991 there were fewer people who called themselves Yugoslavs but the Yugoslav state also by 1991 was simply failing and, therefore, it would be natural that fewer people would feel pro-Yugoslav, or at least for the Yugoslavia they had. The point I was trying to emphasise before, of course, was that the -- the notion that there would be no sort of Yugoslavia at all was a notion which was held by not very many people. People just wanted a different sort of Yugoslavia. The trouble, of course, is that the sort of Yugoslavia that Serbs, Croats, Slovenes, Macedonians, Bosniaks, and so forth might have wanted was never the same sort of Yugoslavia. They couldn't agree on the sort of Yugoslavia it should be.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Wheeler, geographically speaking, what about the different popularity rates? Where was this pro-Yugoslav orientation less popular? Was it less popular in Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina, or in Serbia and Montenegro? Where was it less popular?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, undoubtedly the -- the sort of Yugoslavia that existed in 1990 and 1991 was least popular amongst Slovenes and Croats. Macedonians and most people in Bosnia and Herzegovina were desperately keen to keep Yugoslavia together in some new format, and of course the most radical proponents of an entirely sort of new Yugoslavia was the Serbian government and -- Serbian government in Belgrade and its acolytes in Titograd and Novi Sad, or for that matter, Pristina, who were advocating a different sort of Yugoslavia altogether; a highly centralised Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You said a while ago that on the 25th of June Croatia and Slovenia adopted declarations of independence. Do you know what exactly these regulations enshrined? I'm talking about Croatia now. I'm not mentioning Slovenia because that's of no consequence to us right now. What was the Croats' view about their own representatives in terms of their involvement in the work of the federal bodies that still existed?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Croatian representatives were meant to withdraw.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that this was another nail in the coffin, even de jure now, of this country that at the time was still called the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it certainly was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Wheeler, I'm sure you're familiar with this declaration proclaiming a new sovereign and Independent State of Croatia. This was published in their Official Gazette number 31, page 850, and the date is the 25th of June, 1991. The first thing in this declaration is, bearing in mind the -- the long Croatian tradition, it has preserved its awareness of its own statehood. What about the 13 centuries being referred to? 13 centuries of tradition as a separate state. 13 centuries, as we would call that in Serbia. 13 centuries long, not since the 13th century. The claim is being made here that Croats have had 13 centuries of statehood. What about this notion? Because this strikes me as utterly different from something that I heard from you yesterday, sir.

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The invocation in the Croatian Declaration of Independence of 13 centuries of Croatian statehood is the sort of mythic mumbo-jumbo that all peoples in Central and Eastern Europe are prone to adopt. That doesn't mean there wasn't a real tradition of Croatian statehood, but the idea that it was relevant tradition to the circumstances of 1991 was, of course, nonsense. The important thing in the context was, of course, that there was a Croatian nation. Croatian states had come and gone, but those Croatian states had not been states of any Croatian nation before the 19th century because there was no Croatian nation. There was no French nation. There was no British nation. There was no Serb nation. The idea that we now have about nations is a 19th century creation. So the relevant thing, of course, is that Croats have been self-conscious of themselves as a nation, as a people, since about the 1830s in any case. That's all the -- that's all the Declaration of Independence really would have needed to refer to, that we Croats and the other people who live amongst us are a nation. The invocation of the long medieval tradition, frequently glorious but even more frequently inglorious and obscure, was utterly unnecessary, but that's the kind of rhetoric that most peoples adopt.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: It's some sort of political marketing, wouldn't you say?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Wheeler, you said yesterday that Croatia was recognised as an independent stayed by the EU, if I'm not mistaken, in February, 1992. I may be wrong. Please don't hold that against me.

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was January.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: January. That's right. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the middle of January, and the effect of this was rather spoiled from the point of the -- most of the EU countries' point of view by virtue of the fact the Germans had announced in advance that they would do it on the 15th of January. So in other words, they did it a month early by simply announcing it would happen. And we talked about the reasons why the Germans felt this would be a contribution to a peaceful resolution of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Now that you've mentioned this, Mr. Wheeler, the Germans have this idea that this might lead to a peaceful resolution, let me ask you something else: Was this Germany's sole motive or did they also perhaps mean to reward Croatia for any merits that it may have had in World War II, in World War I, or whatever it was in the past? What was it that drove Germany to leave its bloc, as it were, and to rush ahead of everyone else in terms of this premature international recognition and forcing the hand of the international community? We have this idea of peaceful resolution. The war would stop if we granted Croatia recognition. Was this helpful or did it actually contribute to things getting out of hand?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Germans were ardently in favour of recognising the reality of Slovenia's and Croatia's independence because, as I said, they thought certainly in the case of Croatia it would contribute to ending the war. But there were other reasons as well. One of those, of course, was that there was tremendous popular sentiment in Germany in favour of recognising Croatia's independence, and this has nothing to do whatsoever with an alliance in the Second World War that most Germans, of course, would have had no memory of, but it had much more to do with the fact that Germany itself had just been a huge beneficiary of the process of national self-determination. What, of course, I'm referring to is the unification of East and West Germany. Since the Germans believed in the principle of national self-determination, they believed that that principle should also apply to Croats and Slovenes. Now, you asked me whether not the recognition, when it came, was responsible. I think it was responsible, or would have been responsible, and it might actually even have been helpful had the international community, including Germany, taken any measures at that time to stop what was then the completely predictable spread of the war into Bosnia-Herzegovina. Recognising Croatia was fine, but it was actually an invitation to war in Bosnia and Herzegovina, which, of course, became infinitely the worst of the wars of Yugoslav secession.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: A while ago there was reference to this collective body that ran the state. Mr. Mesic was helped into his seat by the assistance of the European Union, as it were. Mr. Wheeler, you've just mentioned Germany. Germany is keen to help Croatia gain its independence. It's keen to help Slovenia. They think they are right, and indeed they are helping. Do you know if there were perhaps any other foreign countries, foreign services, if you like, foreign organisations, that facilitated Croatia's leaving the community that at the time was still known as the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were other European states that looked benevolently upon the idea of an independent Croatia. Austria was one. I know that there are still an awful lot of people, both in the former Yugoslavia but also abroad, who would like to believe that there were other forces at work, perhaps various intelligence services or the Vatican. I have never seen any evidence to back this up. It's not necessary to invent conspiracies. The situation on the ground was bad enough in its own right to produce the result that it produced.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of any meetings that took place between Mr. Franjo Tudjman and Mr. Milosevic? You mentioned Bosnia. Any talks they had about the division of Bosnia as one of the ways to prevent the spread of a simmering conflict as something that was already in the air, as it were?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very much so. The most famous encounter, of course, between Milosevic and Tudjman took place in Karadjordjevo late in March, 1990. And they did -- excuse me, in 1991. And they did indeed discuss the partition of Bosnia and Herzegovina. This is where we come back to the notion of the significance of the 1939 Banovina. Tudjman himself was wedded to the notion that Croatia should have, in 1991 or 1992, everything that Croatia had had in 1939. Milosevic appears to have led Tudjman to believe that some sort of deal had been struck, but that was almost certainly Tudjman's own fanciful recollections of what he thought he had won. We don't actually have any stenographic record of what happened and what was said at Karadjordjevo. We only have the recollections of various people who were told immediately after the meeting, usually by Tudjman, I'm not aware that -- I can't remember that Jovic, for example, describes this in his book. So we don't know exactly what was decided there but Tudjman certainly went away believing that he and Milosevic had carved up Bosnia-Herzegovina and thereby created a reason for no more -- excuse me, for no more -- for no war to continue or to -- I should say for no war to break out in a serious way in Croatia itself. Tudjman, as a former JNA general, always found it extremely difficult to contemplate a -- a -- any kind of real war with the JNA. He was always looking for means of avoiding overt military confrontations. At least in this phase.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You're quite right, Mr. Wheeler. We don't have any records of that. There is an interview by Mr. Stjepan Mesic where he discusses this, but I'm not going into that right now. There was a bit of bad language being exchanged in those interviews, so I suppose we should just leave this for another occasion perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have several minutes left to go before the break, Your Honours, and there's another topic that I would like to move onto now, Your Honours, for which reason this might be a convenient time to have an early break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Bulatovic. We will resume in 20 minutes' time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: To continue, Mr. Wheeler, we talked about the Yugoslav People's Army insignia, markings, the constitutional role. What I would like to know is the following: You probably followed in the materials that you used and in other ways what the attitude was of Croatia, both the Croatian people and the state representatives towards the Yugoslav People's Army on the territory of the Republic of Croatia. How did they view that Yugoslav People's Army? Was it a favourable view, sympathetic, or was it with antipathy? Could you please tell us.

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Croatian attitude, both the attitude of the Tudjman government in Zagreb and popular attitude, I would guess became increasingly hostile towards the JNA from 1990 through 1991, obviously hostile by 1991. But there had been in Croatia, as there was in the international media, a tendency to want to believe during 1990 and early in 1991 that the JNA would be even-handed and that when it interposed itself in situations that might have led to armed confrontations, that it would be fair. Experience proved otherwise. In other words, when the -- far from being a settler of local conflicts, in the Knin area and Lika, for example, the army tended to intervene on the side of the Serb residents, and so therefore the expectation on the part of Croat villagers or the government in Zagreb towards the army, that attitude became increasingly hostile.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Wheeler, do you remember the attack on members of the Yugoslav People's Army in Split on the 6th of May, 1991, when a JNA soldier was strangled before TV cameras? This was a Macedonian soldier.

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I certainly do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall incidents in front of the military court in Zagreb? Do you remember the blockades of the Bjelovar and Varazdin barracks? Could you explain that phenomenon of, let's say, attacks against the manpower and facilities of the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The -- Tudjman's decision not to fight the JNA but, rather, to seek to disable it by barricading it in its barracks in those areas actually under the government's control was his principal strategy at this time. It was designed to frustrate JNA military operations but also to -- but also to oppose the army in a way that a largely unarmed Croatia, a Croatia without an effective army of its own, could actually accomplish and at the same time win foreign sympathy. Tudjman was, at this point, unlike other members of his government - for example, Martin Spegelj - was very resistant to the idea of any frontal confrontations with the army, and this blockade strategy was what he resorted to instead.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know of Franjo Tudjman's call on the 5th of May, 1991, when he called upon the Croatian economy to switch to the manufacture of weapons in order to fight against the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that particular summons but I do remember pictures that appeared in the press at the time of rather amusing looking homemade tanks and the like. So there was a general effort, certainly in Croatia, to arm by whatever means possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Wheeler, we have a constitutional role. There is a constitution that was still in force. There is also the existence de jure of a state community by the name of Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. We have an army, we have military facilities on the territory of that community, we have members of the Yugoslav People's Army who live and work in those buildings or facilities. They're strangled in Split, barracks are being blockaded, telephone, water, and electricity are being cut off. There is no food. What is the army supposed to do in such a situation? Does it have a legitimate right to use the power at its disposal to deblock its barracks and to help the members of its units there in a situation when the negotiations are obviously not yielding any results? They're not functioning?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're now back into an area of constitutional issues or asking for a legal answer: What is the army supposed to do in this type of a situation? And it appears that they're asking whether it's legal bases in this type of a situation. That is not the type of a question for an historian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I am completely aware of Mr. Wheeler's position, that he's not a constitutional expert, and my questions were not seeking a constitutional or a legal foundation for the army intervention. I'm asking Mr. Wheeler, as an historian who followed all the events, to provide from a historical aspect and from a historical distance an analysis of the events that ensued and to give his opinion and to tell us if he had information or knowledge about the intervention of the army and the reasons for that intervention. I was not asking Mr. Wheeler to provide any answers in relation to constitutional or legal matters. I am asking my question on the basis of Mr. Wheeler having said that he had read the constitution and perhaps then because this is so he can provide answers to the questions that I put.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic, the Chamber feels that your question was somewhat imprecisely seeking to draw on both legal constitutional issues and on, as it were, the merits or options for quasi-political action by a military force in that situation. In either case, it seems beyond the legitimate range of Dr. Wheeler's expertise. So a question of that nature is something you may have to pose to us and leave us to be unguided in an answer at later stage of the trial.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I might actually just venture an opinion in this matter myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think not, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You think not. All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Wheeler, we talked about an army by the name of Yugoslav People's Army. What I would like to know now is something about the Croatian army. When was it formed, who made it up, and what sort of information do you have on that topic?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know very much about the exact process whereby the Croatian army was established. Of course, its first incarnation as the ZNG, Zbor Narodne Garde, that force was formed, I think it was in August of 1991. By the end of 1991, of course, a formal Hrvatska Vojska - Croatian army - was established. So there was a progressive building up of something that could be legitimately called a Croatian army. It was, of course, facilitated by arms smuggling and by desertions of conscripts and officers of Croatian, but also other Yugoslav, citizens from the JNA. At the same time as Tudjman is building up or seeking to create the basis for an army, he's also, of course, created special police units, special forces in the police. That was his first effort. Then the ZNG, the Zbor Narodne Garde, comes next, and finally by the end of 1991, a proper Croatian army. By the end of 1991 a proper Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: The HOS was mentioned. Could you please tell us what HOS is?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The H-O-S, HOS, was a paramilitary formation notable for its black uniforms which evoked the Ustashi. It was loyal as a unit, supposedly, at any rate, to the Party of Rights, and it was a thorn in Tudjman's side because it was outside his control and seemed to be as eager to persecute people, particularly Serbs, as it was to do any effective defending of an independent Croatian state.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: These were followers of the Croatian Party of Rights. Is that the party of Mr. Starcevic or is this a radical wing of that party, the way you described it earlier?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course, Starcevic had been dead for a century. It was a radical party evoking his supposed legacy and at that point it was led by a man called Paraga [Realtime transcript read in error "Praga"], Dobroslav Paraga.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Just an intervention: On the transcript page 36, line 13, it says "Praga," but his name is Paraga. Mr. Wheeler, I know that Mr. Starcevic is dead and this is the Croatian Party of Rights from 1861. We're talking about Paraga. What I would like to know is whether the secretary of that party was Ante Pavelic, whom we mentioned. Of course this was not in the time of Paraga but from before. We're talking about the original party based on which this party emerged.

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Ante Pavelic was -- this is complicated in that there were various strands of Pravastvo in Croatia. One of those elements that claimed descent from Starcevic was the party to which Ante Pavelic belonged back in -- this is in the 1920s.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any information -- you already mentioned the way these Croatian formations were armed. One was the illegal purchase of weapons. Do you know who took part in these illegal arms sales? I'm thinking of Hungary, but do you know of any other country or any other channel for the illegal procurement of weapons by the Croatian armed forces?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The channel that was most often mentioned at the time was certainly the Hungarian one. In the aftermath of the break-up of the Warsaw Pact there was, of course, a huge amount of weaponry sloshing around for purchase all over Eastern Europe, and so it wasn't difficult for the Croatian regime to buy weapons. It was, of course, also aided by the right wing elements in the Croatian diaspora all around the world who contributed money, and presumably we can assume were also themselves sending arms to the embattled homeland.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any information about the Croatian armed forces arming themselves also by taking weapons from blockaded barracks after they were abandoned by members of the JNA, and they were used in order to fight those very same forces of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no knowledge of this, but it certainly would stand to reason that they did so. In other words, it would not surprise me at all if any armaments left behind after negotiated withdrawals by JNA forces from various barracks and camps hadn't been immediately taken advantage of by the nascent Croatian forces. It would be sensible for them to have done so.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to the weapons after the withdrawal of the Yugoslav People's Army from Slovenia through Croatia? Do you know that on that occasion, during the attack on a convoy, the Croatian armed forces confiscated 105 rail cars of -- of weapons as well as other equipment, and this was then kept by the Croatian armed forces?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recollect that specific incident, but as I said in reply to your previous question, it wouldn't surprise me in the slightest that they did so. They would have looked upon any such armaments that they could seize from the JNA as armaments which at least in part had been paid for by Croatian taxpayers in previous years, and they would have regarded it as their rightful possessions. This would have been the case, of course, with each and every one of the Yugoslav peoples. For example, we know that the Slovenes were very, very quick off the mark, when they started setting up their armed forces, in seizing all of the weapons that were in the depots of the Territorial Defence. The Croats were very less good at doing this. They had to make up for lost time and find any means they possibly could of acquiring the weaponry they obviously believed they needed.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Pardon. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Wheeler, do you know that there was an agreement between Slovenia and Croatia on a joint defence after -- joint defence from the JNA, which was signed in April 1991? Kucan signed this agreement with Tudjman. Are you aware of this agreement?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It ended up, of course, being an agreement that neither side honoured.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: And do you know why?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The short answer would be state interest, and that would be because it would have been impossible and dangerous for Croatia to offer support to Slovenia during the 10-day war at the end of June, beginning of July of 1991, and it would have been dangerous and difficult for Slovenia to have offered support to Croatia thereafter when the locus of the war shifts in July to Croatia. There was no love lost between the two capitals and their governments, although it is often said that the Croats did at least, in late June, 1991, seek to stop some JNA columns crossing from Croatia into Slovenia, although as I understand it, that would have been rather irrelevant anyway since there were plenty of JNA troops already in Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Wheeler, the agreement on a joint defence signed between Croatia and Slovenia in April, 1991, and the intervention of the JNA in Slovenia after that, that's when the intervention ensued; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: My question is: If that is so, does that mean that Croatia and Slovenia deliberately prepared this agreement in order to organise in that way and defend themselves from an attack that was already being prepared while we do have an indisputable fact that during that time the Presidency of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was talking and debating, and then after that we have the incidents that took place. So according to you, what would be the motivation for signing such an agreement on a joint defence when there were no attacks that were actually happening? This was in April, 1991. What would be the sense of it?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The principal purpose -- and I'm speculating now. The principal purpose would have been simply to deter any such eventual attack. It would have been to deter the JNA by the threat that there might be more significant resistance than might otherwise have been the case. It also would have been a sop or an encouragement to public morale in both Slovenia and Croatia. In other words, it would have served to make people feel better, to feel braver, to feel safer that they had this supposed agreement, an agreement which, as I've already said, was not actually honoured.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: So could you please explain. We have April, 1991. What were the armed forces at the disposal of Slovenia, what were the armed forces at the disposal of Croatia for them to sign an agreement on a joint defence? What would they use to defend themselves, and who would they defend themselves from if this is so? I'm trying to present this picture. They don't have an army. They don't have any weapons. They don't have any armed formations.

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, by April, 1991, the Slovenes actually did have the making of an army. As I've explained before, they were very successful in getting to Territorial Odbrana - Territorial Defence - arms depots before the JNA did. The Croats, as you suggest, had nothing. They had a police force in which Tudjman did not really believe, and they were only beginning their efforts to create the nucleus of an armed force. And that's why I was saying that the principal purpose of this agreement would have been its potential deterrent effect and its morale-boosting effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Wheeler, I didn't say that the Croats didn't have anything. Quite the contrary. I think that they did have a lot, but it was just presented as them not having much. But in any event, do you know that there was a Presidency session in its full composition, all the members attended which was supposed to attend, and it was held on the 12th of July, 1991, in Belgrade. Do you know that one of the conclusions of that Presidency meeting was to disarm all the paramilitary formations on the territory of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know if that was eventually carried out? If not, why not? Who was it that stood in the way of this decision taken by the Supreme Command being implemented?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The decision was not made in good faith by the principal parties to it. Neither the Serb nor the Croat representative would have intended to carry it out. One would imagine that the representatives from Bosnia and Herzegovina, Macedonia, would have been terribly keen, would have wanted to believe in such a decision, but by July, 1991, neither the Serb nor the Croatian representative would have acted in good faith. It would have been some -- just -- just like the meeting of the Presidency itself at that date, it was something that was done largely for international consumption, particularly consumption by the European Union.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You say that there was no good faith on the Croatian side, or the Serbian side, for that matter, for a decision like that. Within the framework that we have been discussing so far, a JNA representative -- we know that a JNA representative advocated the preservation of the common state. Would they have sincerely backed this decision if they had been given a chance to actually have it implemented?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot and you cannot know for certain, but I would at that stage believe that it would have been highly unlikely that they would have wanted to have that decision implemented on the ground for any Serb paramilitary units. They might have liked to have it implemented for non-Serb paramilitary units.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, let us go back to something we talked about earlier on. We have the HOS, the paramilitary unit; black shirts, black uniforms, Ustasha insignia, the chequerboard. I don't know if I asked you about that too. We have an historical tradition. We have the genocide at the expense of the Serbs and the Jews. What about the panic in Eastern Slavonia? It might have been fed by the media, but was this in fact justified?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We talked about this yesterday, and I agree there was a tremendous amount of justified fear amongst both Serb and Croat communities in Eastern Slavonia and also amongst the respective national minorities. Fear was palpable. As regards the HOS, Tudjman, of course, wanted very desperately to get rid of HOS himself. He actually took steps in the summer of 1991 to get rid of Mercep's paramilitaries, although that -- that actually ended up involving promoting Mercep to a position in the Ministry of Interior, I believe. But in any case, undisciplined forces were not something that his government wanted, but I suppose in the early days they were considered useful, but they became counter-productive. And certainly the Ustasha regalia of the HOS was a deep embarrassment to the Tudjman government. On the other hand, you referred to the Sahovnica, the chequerboard symbol of the Croats. I've never understood myself why the appearance of the Sahovnica on the new Croatian flag and the prominence it was given should have offended anybody because, of course, the Sahovnica had been on the coat of arms of the Socialist Republic of Croatia since 1946. The fact that it was given increased prominence I suppose was emblematic of the nationalistic tenor of the Tudjman regime, but the Sahovnica itself was not something that ought to have been offensive to Serbs in any respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Wheeler, in addition the chequerboard, do you know if the HOS included any other markings or insignia on their uniforms that might have been construed as being linked to the Ustasha movement?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think some individuals enjoyed having the U, the Ustasha U, on their uniforms. They were also notable for doing things that the Ustasha hadn't done; they liked to wear lots of rosaries around their necks. But I can't remember anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what rosaries we are talking about. Can you explain that, please.

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Rosary beads, Catholic rosary beads for saying "Hail Mary" prayers with the crucifix of the Bahaman beads around that you number and pass through your fingers. They became ostentatious symbols of the religiosity that accompanied this effusion of Croatian nationalism in these years. And dark glasses. These HOS guys were not a pretty sight.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: We have the JNA, we have the Territorial Defence. You say Slovenia seized the TO weapons but Croatia didn't. It was late in doing this. So what was done was done. The role of the TO within the system of the armed forces, do you know how that worked, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depend -- it depended -- the relationship of the TO to the JNA depended upon whether or not there was a state of war or not. It came under the direct control of the JNA in a time of crisis or war. I can't remember the exact circumstances that were provided for by law. But in time of peace, of course, it was under the control of the respective republican governments. And what was happening with the TO units in these months and years was that they were fracturing, dividing themselves up just, of course, like Yugoslavia itself was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: What happens to the TO units that are still in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The TO units in Croat majority areas would have formed, in terms of their manpower, the nucleus for a future Croatian army.
