But as we've already discussed, they had very little of the original TO weaponry at their disposal since the JNA had been efficient enough to seize most of this weaponry before the Croats themselves had a chance to seize it. Of course, in Serb majority areas, the TO weaponry had all been taken by the local Serb militias. And in mixed areas like Eastern Slavonia, they -- the Territorial Odbrana was divided up into its national components, and I assume the weaponry was as well, although we have reason to believe, I suppose, that most of it went to the Serb part of the former TO organisations.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: These decisions taken by the TO on separation and singling out, as you've just described, these are entirely illegitimate, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I object, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think this time, Mr. Weiner, it's Mr. Bulatovic's question can be seen as sufficiently legitimate in view of the opinions being expressed to this point. Carry on, Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Shall I answer the question, Mr. Bulatovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, if you can.

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think it was illegitimate. But as we have already established many times over, an awful lot of illegitimate things were happening in Yugoslavia at this time. Things which from the point of view of the law or the point of view of constitutional niceties, were extremely illegitimate, but they were happening, nonetheless, all over the place. And that's what happens when a country falls apart and certainly when a war begins.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Wheeler, we've heard your evidence. This is something you confirmed and I can't contradict you on this: The JNA was structured in a certain way, its ethnic make-up was what it was, kept all of its insignia and seemed bent on preserving a Yugoslav community. This being the principal notion and the idea behind the JNA, would it not seem as their legitimate right to take action or intervene in a certain area, granted the rights that they enjoyed under the constitution, an area that was still formally and officially part of what was then still called the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'd object, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic, you're manoeuvering back around to the same line of questioning, aren't you. I let you go as far as I might with that question a few minutes ago, but now I think you're back onto improper territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I accept that, Your Honour. I accept that objection -- or, rather, I accept your guidance about this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Wheeler, just to wrap it up, bearing in mind all these various aspects that we have covered, historical aspects, constitutional aspects, and the very facts themselves, the facts that pertained to this complex multinational community with a lot of different and divergent interests at stake, bearing in mind further the role of the JNA, how it was made up, what its guiding principles were, and all of that; bearing in mind the Presidency of the SFRY which worked in the way that it did, which made decisions in the way that it did; bearing in mind the role of JNA representatives in the work of the Presidency, which is something you have described for us, their role being to preserve Yugoslavia; bearing all that in mind, could the Yugoslav army have been misused to carry out certain assignments that it was given and that the army simply had to carry out under the system that prevailed at the time, these having been assignments given by their commanders?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. The Yugoslav People's Army was an army by June, 1991, that no longer had a state to fight for, to defend, and to uphold. That state was dying. I would argue, in fact, that by the end of June, 1991, that state was dead. Therefore, the JNA was an army without a state. This is an insight which we owe a long time ago to Milos Vasic, the principal expert on military affairs in Serbia, or for that matter, in the former Yugoslavia. And as an army without a state, it needed to find a new cause, a new master, a new state to serve. And given the fact that it was haemorrhaging in terms of desertions, non-Serbs from its ranks and from its officer corps, it's hardly surprising that that new state it wanted to serve was the variously imagined or configured Greater Serbia that Slobodan Milosevic appeared at that time to favour. In other words, Greater Serbia was the fallback position for the JNA in the absence of a socialist Yugoslav state that it could legitimately defend. That does not alter the fact -- in other words, what I'm trying to say is that the JNA had no place else to go other than to give its loyalty to the Milosevic regime. The odd thing about this, of course, is that we now know the extent to which Milosevic himself never trusted the JNA and subsequently put all his efforts into creating a Serbian -- well, excuse me, a Serbian -- it's -- I'm trying to find the right word. Special forces of the Serbian MUP of the Ministry of the Interior. In other words, he created an alternative army which was uniquely under his control because he never trusted the old Yugoslavia ethos that prevailed at the top of the JNA. The JNA, for him, was always a dubious element, even when it was transformed in 1992 into the Vojska Jugoslavija, the VJ.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: That is precisely the reason I'm asking. Is it possible, the constellation being what it was, that the army did not suit someone who was in power and that these powers that be may have used the army in order to discredit the army itself and provide a convenient justification for something else that was eventually done?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I object to that, Your Honour. It's not clear what the question is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It actually stems from something I wrote in my report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I don't agree, Mr. Weiner. Please go ahead, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Actually, I agree with you, Mr. Bulatovic. I believe that the army was misused and it was intentionally misused, and Milosevic bragged often about it. He told Jovic in spring of 1990, "We will -- we will subvert this army and bend it to our own purposes." And that process continued throughout Milosevic's time in power under whatever -- holding whatever office he supposedly held. So the army was, it seems to me, subverted and traduced and destroyed by the destruction of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe there's an error in the transcript. Page 48, line 13. I think this should read 1991 and not 1990, as the transcript reflects.

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the error was mine. I probably said 1990. In fact -- no, I'm sure it was spring, 1990, in fact. That's right. Very early, in other words.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: My apologies, then. It must have been a misinterpretation. Mr. Wheeler, your last answer being what it is about Slobodan Milosevic and that faction of the Serbian leadership through which he allegedly exercised power not believing in the JNA or having misgivings about the JNA, can we agree that in 1991, Slobodan Milosevic and this leadership did not support or indeed back the constitutional position of the JNA as it was simply because it did not fit the bill of the Greater Serbian policies? This is what is usually written about this topic, what is suggested.

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. I agree completely. And going back to the previous question, of course, it is often argued that one of the principal reasons why the decision was made to send the JNA on a fruitless mission to take control of Slovenia's borders in -- on the 27th of June, 1991, was precisely to discredit that army and leave it with no option but in future to do the bidding of Milosevic. It was to destroy the JNA as a Yugoslav army and, in the process, leave the army with no alternative but loyalty to Milosevic. But as I said before, Milosevic always doubted the loyalty of that army, and its successor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you this, sir: There is a particular section in your report where you suggest that the JNA occupied some of the territory and carried out acts of ethnic cleansing. Is this language not in fact a little too strong? Based on everything we have heard and the JNA's general orientation being what it was, could not possibly have occupied any territory in their own territory, least of all, then, commit any acts of ethnic cleansing in their territory.

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here we're into a legal minefield. Was it their own territory in the autumn of 1991? I don't -- I don't think in practical terms it was. Now, the use of the term "ethnic cleansing" may be unfortunate because the term hadn't yet come into common parlance, but operations in Baranja, around Ilok and various other villages surrounding Vukovar, certainly bore the characteristics of what we would later happily -- excuse me, "happily" is the wrong word -- of what we would later commonly call "ethnic cleansing." The trouble with the idea of this being carried out by the country's own army on its own territory is at the very heart of the problem which the army itself faced, but of course all those with whom it came into contact faced. Whose army was it anyway? Whose country was it anyway? That was, of course, what the war was about.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: We will agree, though, that these were areas of combat operations, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I wish to thank Mr. Wheeler. I have finished my cross-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Bulatovic. Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Just a few questions in redirect, Your Honour. May the witness be shown paragraph 104, which is the section on page 38 from the decision in Prosecutor versus Tadic, which is IT-94-1-T, and it concerns part of the cross-examination by Mr. Sljivancanin's attorney in relation to Mr. Kadijevic, the ethnic make-up of the JNA, and the JNA itself in 1991, and I would just like to show that to the witness. It's on page 38, and it's quoting "My View of the Break-up, An Army Without a State," by General Kadijevic. It begins the last two words down from the third line on the top. Third line from the top, last two words. If you can ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'll read this to you on page 38.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Slowly, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Very slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Of the JNA, he writes that: "By 1991, it was no longer an army with a cohesive state to defend; the state which it was its duty to defend was disintegrating and just as its ranks were now substantially filled with ethnic Serbs, so its task in the immediate future would be to regroup its forces and equipment, scattered throughout the former Yugoslavia including the seceding republics, back into what was left of the nation and then to concentrate upon the protection and defence of those ethnic Serbs who in the course of this disintegration found themselves outside of Serbia and Montenegro. This, it was envisioned would lead ultimately to the creation of a new substantially Serb, Yugoslavia, with its core in Serbia and Montenegro but including also parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina and Croatia principally but not exclusively those parts presently having as majority Serb population." Could you comment on that, please?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It seems to me that's a wholly accurate description of what was happening and what would -- what the regime would seek to put in place.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Had the ethnic make-up of the army changed by 1991, and why?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I just told Mr. Bulatovic -- or reminded him, rather -- I'm sure he didn't need it, though -- the ethnic composition of the army was changing dramatically in the course of 1991. As I said, it was losing through desertion many of its -- most, in fact, of its non-Serb conscripts. Non-Serb officers were also leaving. And it was also having tremendous difficulties carrying out any conscription, even in Serbia and Montenegro. So it was generally terribly, terribly weakened in terms of manpower.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: On a manpower basis, how did the JNA make up for this loss of -- of soldiers through desertion?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, one practical remedy, of course, was to rely increasingly upon so-called volunteers. These were paramilitary formations that were either local to the area of operations involved or which came directly from Serbia, some of which were under the patronage of one or another political party, others might have been creations of the state -- Serbian state security structures. So we had increasing JNA reliance, in its weakened state, upon volunteers, paramilitaries, and, where relevant, the remnants of the old Territorial Defence system.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: From July of 1991 to the end of November, 1991, in Eastern Slavonia, in Croatia, which includes the Vukovar area, were TO and paramilitary members or soldiers used by the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were certainly used, and they were used for what one might call the dirty work.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And what is the dirty work?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The dirty work was the actual entry into hostile -- or villages or towns that were thought to be hostile and carrying out what, as I said in a previous answer, was later to be called ethnic cleansing. That is committing random or carefully targeted murders, it could be either, but the general purpose of which was to cause the bulk of the alien population to flee, to flee for its lives.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And were you aware during the same time period, July through -- July 1 through the end of November, or November 22, 1991 - so July 1, 1991, through to the end of November, 1991 - in Eastern Slavonia, which includes Vukovar, were you aware or did you learn of Serb TOs and paramilitaries working jointly with the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now -- now, you were questioned about Croats obtaining weaponry. In that same time period, July through November, the weaponry that the Croats had, was that comparable to the weaponry of the JNA with their TOs and paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at all. The disproportion in the arms and ammunition available to the JNA and the paramilitary forces working with it was -- the disproportion was very, very great. In other words, the JNA and its acolytes had vastly far more firepower available to them than did the local Croat defenders or the Croat army that was being created.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And were the numbers of forces between the two groups - the Croats on one hand and the JNA, the TOs, and paramilitaries working together - were those numbers of forces capable in that same time period, July through November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner, are you asking about Vukovar alone? Because, of course, by the late summer of 1991, Vukovar, the heart of the town, is effectively surrounded and besieged, and that meant that there were defenders there, small numbers of them. Estimates usually say there were between 1.000 and 1.500 by, say, late August of 1991. They were tiny in comparison to the forces that were investing Vukovar, the JNA forces, and their various helpmates. But that doesn't mean that in other areas of the battlefield elsewhere in Croatia there might not have been places where the numbers were rather more equal, especially if we were talking about Western Slavonia or Banija where JNA involvement, certainly in Banija, was less common and, therefore, the contention might have been more roughly equivalent bands of fighters. But wherever the JNA was, of course, it had overwhelming numerical and ordnance -- ordnance superiority.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, just one more area. The fact that the JNA has traditionally been an all people's national defence, would that make it not -- would that make it usual or not unusual for the JNA to rely on TO members and paramilitaries and volunteers?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's very important to make a distinction between paramilitaries on the one hand and the Territorial Defence on the other. The Territorial Defence was the active reserve of the Yugoslav state. It was a throwback to Partisan doctrine of all people's national defence. It was composed of people who were trained and had exercises regularly and were -- and who were subordinated to the army's command in all situations of emergency. The paramilitaries were a completely new phenomenon and one which was to -- not even to the taste of very many JNA officers who regarded them as a bloodthirsty, drunken, whoring, rape-inclined rabble.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: However were they still used by the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER [Resumed]
utterances.text: They certainly were. There was no alternative but to use them. So it was felt at the time, anyway. Because the JNA commanders could not trust their own forces at that point to engage in really hard fighting, certainly not street fighting, hand-to hand fighting, house-to-house fighting because of the rampant problems with desertion and very low morale. So the JNA contented itself to use its advantages of massive firepower and, as I said before, let these paramilitary types do the dirty work.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And does that include the area of Eastern Slavonia and Vukovar between July, 1991, and November 22nd -- I'm sorry, November 22nd, 1991?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It -- it certainly does.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Weiner. Well, Doctor, you'll be pleased to know that's the end of the exercise. The Chamber is grateful for your assistance and for your trouble in attending here. You are, of course, now free to return to your other interests. Thank you indeed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I would like to use this time after the witness has left to say on behalf of all the three Defence teams, to talk about the topic initiated yesterday regarding the testimony of Mr. Kostovic and Mr. Hrabac, whose statements we received and which relate to the documents that Ms. Bosanac brought with her when she testified on the last occasion. As far as the written statements are concerned, the Defence teams have nothing against the Prosecution tendering them, according to Rule 89(F), the way they are, but we do believe that there is a need to cross-examine the witness in view of the matters that he's talking about and the information that we were given here, which we believe is relevant in relation to the indictment. I know that you left it to us 'til Monday to provide a written response, but I don't know if you would accept this oral response by the Defence teams, because I believe that we will be more -- contributing to a more efficient proceedings in this way. Today we received another written request from our learned friends to amend the 65 ter list with a new witness. We would like permission to provide our answer to this request in writing, because it does seem to be a continuation of the practice that the Prosecution has already instituted in relation to previous two witnesses, Ms. Hartmann and Mr. Aric. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Vasic. With respect to the first two witnesses, as I understand it, you'd be happy for their statements to be tendered, but you would like them for cross-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is right, Your Honour. If our learned friends want to tender their statements, that is fine, but we do ask for the opportunity to cross-examine them. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. It seems, Mr. Weiner, it will be necessary to call those two witnesses. I know Mr. Moore was hoping to avoid that. With respect to the request to amend the 65 ter list, you want to submit written submissions, Mr. Vasic. That can be done by Monday, can it?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence could try to do it by Monday, but that might be a considerable effort. We do have an important witness on Monday via video-conference so we would be very grateful to the Trial Chamber if we could have a few more days. Perhaps a day the week after the next to carry this out in view of the fact that we do have an important witness that we need to focus on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, we feel that, despite the pressures on you, certainly it should be feasible by Wednesday of next week to have your written submissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, for your understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We have no more witnesses, I've been told.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You mean we're to have an early day today?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: An early day and an early weekend start.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. I would indicate to the parties that it is expected that the Chamber will file this afternoon its decision on the interpretation of the indictment, which will be of relevance to both parties. In the circumstances, then, we will now adjourn. Could I mention one further matter? It seems that the hours we have set in the hope of moving this case along more quickly have proved of some difficulty to a number of affected interests, so that from now on on Mondays we will resume at 12.30 rather than 12.00 to allow a more appropriate timing for lunch before we commence the hearing, because there's no time during the hearing for a full lunch break. And on the other days, we will extend the lunch break by 15 minutes, to an hour and a quarter, because there were difficulties for a number of people with merely an hour. We will now adjourn until Monday at 12.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 22nd day of May, 2006, at 12.30 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 12.06 p.m.,
